title: Piano Concerto No. 1 in D minor
hook: A young man’s storm that began as a symphony and was hissed at its second performance.

painting.title: Storm at the Coast
painting.pairingNote: Painted in 1855 by the leading landscape painter of Düsseldorf, the city where Brahms was then living near Clara Schumann and turning his stormy symphony into this concerto.

facts: Brahms began the music in 1854, in his early twenties, as a sonata for two pianos. It grew into a symphony, then, in 1855–56, into a piano concerto. He finished it in 1858, after years of advice from his friend the violinist Joseph Joachim, who helped him with the orchestra.

Those were the years of Robert Schumann’s breakdown. Schumann, Brahms’s mentor, was taken to an asylum in 1854 and died there in 1856. Brahms stayed close to his wife, Clara, and many listeners hear that grief in the concerto.
Brahms played the solo part at the first performance, in Hanover on 22 January 1859. The audience was cool. Five days later in Leipzig it was hissed. It took years for the concerto to be accepted.

It is a concerto on the scale of a symphony. The first movement alone lasts over 20 minutes, the piano often works inside the orchestra rather than in front of it, and there is no showy [[cadenza|cadenza]] in the first movement.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a tragic storm (I), a hushed prayer (II), a fierce chase that breaks through into D major (III).

movements.heading: Maestoso
movements.summary: The orchestra opens with a thunderous drum roll and a wild, jagged theme. When the piano finally enters, after more than three minutes, it does so quietly, with a new idea of its own. The movement is a vast [[sonata-form|sonata form]] with a [[double-exposition|double exposition]]. Its noblest tune belongs to the piano alone, and the ending is tragic, not triumphant.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1, the storm
mainIdeas.description: a leaping, angular theme in violins and cellos over a roll of timpani, with fierce [[trill|trill]]s.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2a
mainIdeas.description: a sad, swinging tune, first heard quietly in the orchestra.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2b
mainIdeas.description: a broad, noble melody in F major, played by the piano alone, rising like a hymn.

stops.hear: A low rumble of timpani and basses; violins and cellos hurl out a jagged theme with harsh trills
stops.happening: Theme 1, over a [[pedal-note|pedal note]] on D

stops.hear: Quieter: a sad, swinging tune in the strings, then the oboe
Violent upward rushes in the low strings; the opening theme returns, passed between instruments, horns blazing
stops.happening: The storm again, building to the end of the orchestra’s section

stops.hear: A bright, leaping fanfare in D major
stops.happening: The closing idea of the orchestra’s [[exposition|exposition]]

stops.hear: The piano enters softly, alone, with a new, gentle phrase
stops.happening: The solo exposition begins. The piano does not start with Theme 1

stops.hear: The piano takes up the storm theme’s trills in powerful octaves
Slower and calm; the piano alone plays a noble, rising melody in rich chords
stops.happening: Theme 2b, in F major. Brahms kept this tune for the piano

stops.hear: The strings sing the same noble melody while the piano decorates around it
After a dreamlike hush, the piano crashes in with loud double octaves
A huge climax for full orchestra, then the drum roll and the opening theme, with the piano now leading
stops.happening: The [[recapitulation|recapitulation]]. The theme returns with new, darker harmony

stops.hear: The noble melody once more, now in D major
The sad, swinging tune from the start, at last in D minor, played by the piano

stops.label: Last 45 seconds
stops.hear: Hammering octaves in the piano, the orchestra driving to loud D minor chords

notice: When the piano first enters, it does not play the storm theme. It begins something new and quiet, as if it had a different story to tell.
Listen for the timpani. Brahms uses them far more than was usual, from the first rumble to the last chord.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Curzon and Szell recorded the concerto with the London Symphony Orchestra in Kingsway Hall in 1962, for Decca; the producer was John Culshaw. On the Spotify album the concerto is tracks 1–3, followed by works by Franck and Litolff.

movements.heading: Adagio
movements.summary: After the storm, a prayer. [[muted|Muted]] strings and bassoons play a slow, hymn-like melody, and the piano answers alone, almost in a whisper. Under the opening notes in his manuscript Brahms wrote the words of the *Benedictus*, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord”. The movement is quiet almost throughout and ends with a short, inward [[cadenza|cadenza]] for the piano.

mainIdeas.name: The hymn
mainIdeas.description: a broad, slow melody in muted violins and violas, with bassoons moving gently below.

mainIdeas.name: The piano’s answer
mainIdeas.description: a quiet, prayer-like theme in soft chords, played alone.

stops.hear: Muted strings play a slow, solemn melody; bassoons wind gently beneath
stops.happening: The hymn. The words *Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini* fit these notes

stops.hear: The orchestra falls silent; the piano enters alone, very softly
The strings return quietly; the piano answers with rippling, rhapsodic figures
stops.happening: A dialogue, piano alone and strings alone in turn

stops.hear: Two clarinets play a mournful melody in thirds over the piano
stops.happening: The darker middle section, in B minor

stops.hear: The hymn returns, on oboe and cellos
The piano builds to a loud, rich climax, horns and low strings beneath
stops.happening: The emotional peak of the movement

stops.hear: The piano alone, free and slow, with trills high up

stops.label: Last 2 minutes
stops.hear: The orchestra takes over gently; the piano falls silent; soft chords in D major

notice: Sing the words to the opening melody: “Be-ne-dic-tus qui ve-nit”. They fit the notes. Brahms often called Schumann “Mynheer Domini”, and many hear the movement as a memorial to him; Brahms also described it as a portrait of Clara.

movements.heading: Rondo: Allegro non troppo
movements.summary: The piano starts alone with a fierce, leaping theme in D minor, and the orchestra roars back. This is a [[rondo|rondo]]: the theme keeps returning between contrasting episodes. All the themes share a rising shape. There is a hushed [[fugato|fugato]] in the strings, two short cadenzas, and in the end the music breaks into D major.

mainIdeas.name: The rondo theme
mainIdeas.description: a fast, leaping, aggressive tune, first in the piano alone.

mainIdeas.name: The second theme
mainIdeas.description: noble and rising, in F major, again for the piano alone.

mainIdeas.name: The third theme
mainIdeas.description: gentle and yearning, in the strings.

stops.hear: The piano alone hurls out a leaping, energetic theme
stops.happening: The rondo theme, in D minor

stops.hear: The full orchestra takes it up
The piano alone, a noble rising melody, growing steadily louder
stops.happening: The second theme, in F major

stops.hear: The leaping theme again in the piano
The strings play a gentle, yearning tune; the piano rests
stops.happening: The third theme, in B-flat major

stops.hear: Hushed strings enter one after another on the same busy figure
stops.happening: A [[fugato|fugato]] built from the third theme

stops.hear: A crashing piano descent, then the orchestra blazes out the rondo theme
stops.happening: The rondo theme at full power

stops.hear: The piano alone: rising waves, then a long trill
The key brightens to D major; the horn and piano answer each other
stops.happening: The music turns to the major

stops.hear: Slower, like a calm country march, with a held bass like bagpipes
A brief flourish for the piano alone

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: A trill, the theme in D major, and hammered chords for the whole orchestra

notice: Compare the end of this movement with the end of the first. The first movement ends in D minor, in tragedy; the finale breaks through to D major.

threads.title: A symphony in disguise
threads.body: The concerto began as a symphony, and it shows: the orchestra is a full partner, and the piano often plays inside the texture instead of over it.

threads.title: Schumann
threads.body: The first movement’s storm, the second movement’s *Benedictus* and its portrait of Clara: the concerto was written in the shadow of Robert Schumann’s illness and death.

threads.title: The rising shape
threads.body: The noble piano melody of the first movement climbs upward; the themes of the finale all share that rising shape.

threads.title: Minor to major
threads.body: D minor rules the first movement and the start of the finale; the concerto ends in D major.
